newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Death toll confirmed at 19 in Puerto Rico blast.
newsitem.headline: Death toll confirmed at 19 in Puerto Rico blast.

text.p: Search teams pulled a woman's body from the debris of a shop on Friday, bringing to 19 the confirmed death toll from a blast in a San Juan commercial district apparently caused by a gas leak.
It was the first sign of a body in more than 30 hours of searching that was hampered by torrential rains and the unsafe condition of the ruined building in the Rio Piedras district.
Seventeen bodies were counted in the immediate aftermath of the explosion at the Humberto Vidal shoe shop in Calle de Diego on Thursday morning. About 70 people were wounded.
Another person also died of injuries from the blast in a San Juan hospital on Friday, Police Superintendent Pedro Toledo said.

Sniffer dogs located the body of the 19th victim in La California, a store next to the Humberto Vidal. The unidentified body, of a woman 40 to 45, was put under a paramedics' tent in the courtyard of a church.
Juan Rivera Cancel, leader of the dog team, said, "We think maybe there's more people in there."

Eleven people, probably dead, were believed to be entombed in the ruins of Humberto Vidal so the discovery of a victim in the neighbouring La California building, which had been believed empty, raised fears of an even higher death toll from the gas explosion.
"Reports from owners told us the building was empty," Toledo said.

Relatives of those missing waited in the church. Doris Velez had thought her brother Norberto might be the victim brought out. When told it was not, she sat down on a church pew in tears and phoned relatives on a mobile telephone.

Dog teams and search crews probed a small sector of the gutted six-story Humberto Vidal Building, but they were unable to enter its depths because of its dangerous state. Engineers worked all day propping up the sagging sides with steel girders to prevent it from collapsing on rescue teams.
They still needed to support an unsteady central column, but were doubtful that could be done before nightfall.

Under intermittent torrential rains, with the smell of corpses in the air, dozens of search workers, including teams from Miami and New York, were removing rubble with their bare hands and filling up buckets and passing them back.

Miami's Metro-Dade Fire Rescue FL Task Force One, a veteran of the Oklahoma City bombing and disasters in Colombia, Armenia and the Phillipines, rushed to Puerto Rico as soon as the extent of the tragedy was known.
Metro-Dade team member Chris Martindale, 24, of Pembroke Pines, Florida, resting with two colleagues in a garage after finishing a shift, said the work was grueling.
"It's a big mess. There's no place to start. You have to get everything out by buckets," he said. "And rain makes it more unsafe than it already is."
Martindale said he had seen blood and body parts, and said he could tell there were more bodies in the ruins.

Investigative teams looking into the cause of the blast also were delayed by the building's instability. Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello, visiting the site, said it appeared to have been the result of a gas explosion.
"All evidence so far indicates the explosion was caused by a gas leak. There is no evidence whatsoever it was a criminal act," he said.
